description: We are a team of passionate innovators united by our curiosity for science, technology, and space exploration. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to tackle real-world challenges, explore creative solutions, and turn ambitious ideas into meaningful results. We believe in the power of teamwork, innovation, and pushing boundaries to shape a better future.
summary:
FUSE is a web dashboard in English and Turkish. It turns NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) archive of microgravity combustion experiments into fire-safety insight for crewed missions. It syncs all 133 PSI records, 2,009 experimental test rows and 2,262 publications. It then ranks 19 curated combustion investigations, including BASS, Saffire, FLEX, ACME BRE and SAME, against the atmosphere a crew will actually live in: the ISS, a lunar base, a pressurized rover, a Mars habitat or a spacesuit.

A transparent, deterministic formula does the ranking, not SI, and every part of each score is shown on screen. FUSE also lists coverage gaps, meaning the conditions no experiment has tested yet. An SI agent explains the results, and its numbers, citations and claims about records are checked against NASA data before the user sees them.

FUSE covers all three goals of the challenge: it finds the most relevant research, gives open CSV/JSON data for modeling, and connects findings to fire controls and equipment. This matters because a lunar base at 30% O₂ and 10.2 psi is far more flammable than Earth air. Yet PSI contains no solid-material burn test above 22.2% oxygen. That gap points straight to the experiment NASA should fund next.
details:
What it does
FUSE (Fire Understanding in Space Environments) is a web dashboard in English and Turkish. It helps mission designers, fire-safety engineers, researchers and students use NASA’s microgravity combustion data for crewed exploration. The user picks a habitat (ISS, lunar surface habitat, pressurized rover, Mars habitat, spacesuit or Earth), or sets oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity and a fire-safety focus (prevention, detection or suppression). Every number on the page updates as they do.

How it works

Data: FUSE syncs NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI): 133 investigation records, 22 experimental tables with 2,009 test rows, and 2,262 publications. Tested oxygen, pressure and flow ranges are read straight from the PSI test tables. A curated layer of 19 combustion investigations adds details, and each detail is tied to an exact NASA quote. Automated tests look up every quote in its source. Of 173 curated fields, 148 trace to NASA records. The other 25 are marked as assumptions.

Ranking: A transparent, deterministic formula scores each investigation against the chosen atmosphere. It weighs oxygen, material, flow, focus, pressure, and scale/data. Same input, same result. Every score component and its reason is shown.

Coverage gaps: Rules list the conditions no experiment has reached. For a lunar base (30% O₂, 10.2 psi, 0.165 g), FUSE finds five gaps. For the ISS it finds none.

SI agent: On request, an SI agent reads records, test tables and paper abstracts, then writes an interpretation with live charts and tables embedded. The agent never decides results. Code checks its output first: each cited record must actually have been retrieved, each number with a unit must trace back to the data, and each material or hardware claim is checked against the record.

Other pages: side-by-side comparison, a hardware atlas, design-control guidance, applications on Earth, and open CSV/JSON downloads for modeling.

Key finding and impact
No solid material in PSI has been burned above 22.2% O₂, and none below 14.7 psi. A lunar base will be filled with fabrics and plastics at 30% O₂. ACME BRE suggests that in oxygen-rich, still air, simply shutting off ventilation may not put out a fire. FUSE points to the next experiment NASA should fund: real cabin materials at low pressure and high oxygen, ideally in partial gravity (LUCI, FM2). On Earth, the same data informs smoke detection, water-mist suppression, firefighter equipment and fire models.

Creativity

Formulas do the ranking instead of SI.

Showing “where the data ends” is a main output, not a footnote.

The SI agent is audited by deterministic checks.

Color carries physics: blue (~431 nm CH*, the color of a flame in orbit) stands for microgravity and data, and orange (~589 nm sodium, the color of a flame on Earth) stands for the scenario. Because flames don’t flicker in microgravity, nothing in the interface flickers either.

Tools
TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Radix UI, Motion, D3, KaTeX, nuqs, zod, PostgreSQL (full-text search), Vercel AI SDK with configurable SI providers, Vitest, Docker Compose and GitHub Actions CI.

Factors we considered
Scientific traceability; honesty about what is unknown (partial gravity, unspecified cabin conditions, the rover atmosphere being an assumption); reproducibility (one-command Docker setup and an offline data snapshot); accessibility (contrast checks); cost and abuse limits on the SI agent; and privacy.

Use of SI
An SI agent is part of FUSE and writes interpretations of NASA PSI records. Deterministic code computes all rankings, gaps and unit conversions, and checks the agent’s citations, numbers and record claims. The team used SI coding assistants as tools for writing and reviewing code and documentation. The concept, method, data rules and curation are the team’s own. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used.
